title: Central Bank bars EY partners from bank audits after NDB fraud | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 10 November 2026 00:54
-     - 29

CoPF Chairman SJB MP 

Dr. Harsha de Silva

CBSL Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe

The Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) has barred the Ernst & Young (EY) partners who audited National Development Bank (NDB) from carrying out any further banking audits and forced the lender to reconstitute its Board audit committee, after a Rs. 13.6 billion fraud ran for three years before being uncovered once the 2025 accounts had been certified.

“We have already taken action against the auditors,” Director of Banking Supervision R. R. de Silva Jayatillake told the Committee on Public Finance (CoPF), chaired by SJB MP Dr. Harsha de Silva, on 5 November. “The partners involved cannot continue doing banking audits. We have also got the bank to reconstitute the Board audit committee.”

The reconstitution of the committee and other Board

committees was notified to the Colombo Stock Exchange, officials told the Committee, a disclosure Dr. de Silva said had passed largely unnoticed.

Jayatillake said the regulator had required the bank to submit a rectification timeline, was monitoring progress against it, and was conducting spot examinations.

The findings of the forensic audit were also being used to assess the fitness and propriety of individuals and to decide whether further orders or restrictions were needed.

The auditors flagged the fraud with an asterisk rather than a formal qualification or an emphasis of matter. Members were told those who carried out the fraud were largely compliant with reporting requirements and gave regulators, and possibly the auditors, the run around.

Dr. de Silva pressed the Director on whether the Central Bank was satisfied with the forensic audit carried out by Deloitte, a report the committee has not been given. “You shared some basic points,” he said. Jayatillake replied that the exercise was a forensic audit and that relevant third parties had been interviewed.

Sri Lanka Accounting and Auditing Standards Monitoring Board (SLAASMB) Chairperson E. H. Mohotty told the committee her board’s separate inquiry into auditor conduct was complete and had been referred to the Attorney General on 15 October, 2026, for a view on legal action.

“What SLAASMB looked at is purely on the auditing standards and how well the auditor performed the duties based on the auditing standards,” she said. Asked whether she could disclose the findings, she said: “I think it is not.”

“That means it is scary,” Dr. de Silva said. He added that the Deloitte exercise had looked at NDB’s transactions rather than at the audit firm.

Central Bank Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe said the Bank Supervision Department was working through the SLAASMB report to establish what action could follow. “Basically, they have identified certain individuals,” he said. “They have to look at whether the bank has taken actions against those individuals through the forensic audit.”

He said the regulator was willing to set out in detail the supervisory changes made across the sector since the fraud. “I think we can share in detail what Bank Supervision as a regulator has done to strengthen the process, not only at NDB but also other banks, based on the learning of this incident,” Dr. Weerasinghe said.

Banks have been directed to tighten reconciliation of suspense accounts, he said. “Broader actions, I think we can share with you. That’s not an issue.”

Dr. de Silva said the opacity around specific enforcement was difficult to defend in a regulated financial sector. “I don’t think this can be completely confidential, and it is good to have some sort of transparency,” he said. “I’m not saying give names, but what action you have taken, so that people would feel safe that their money is safe.”

The committee would accept material on confidential cover and proceed on the Attorney General’s advice, he said.

The Central Bank moved against NDB in early April, ordering restrictions on dividends, discretionary payments and branch expansion to protect the bank’s stability, issuing a regulatory statement to assure liquidity and publishing press notices on the institution’s condition. It then required the bank to commission the external forensic audit.

title: Budget reaches Rs. 22.3 b surplus in 9M supported by vehicle import revenue | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 10 November 2026 00:53
-     - 8

The Government’s Budget recorded a surplus of Rs. 22.3 billion in the first nine months of 2026, reversing a deficit of Rs. 441.4 billion a year earlier, as revenue from motor vehicle imports drove a 20% increase in collections that outran a slower rise in spending.

This is according to the latest Finance, Planning and Economic Development Ministry’s Fiscal Review Report.

Revenue excluding grants rose to Rs. 4,594.9 billion from Rs. 3,827.0 billion, while total expenditure increased 7.1% to Rs. 4,579.3 billion from Rs. 4,276.3 billion. The Ministry attributed the turnaround to the revenue increase ‘together with the rationalization of government expenditure’.

Total revenue and grants of Rs. 4,601.6 billion reached 86.8% of the Rs. 5,300 billion annual estimate, while expenditure stood at 60.6% of the Rs. 7,557 billion provision.

The nine-month surplus conceals a deterioration in the closing month.

September recorded a deficit of Rs. 13.1 billion, the first monthly shortfall since July, after a surplus of about Rs. 145 billion in August, according to figures in the previous month’s report.

Monthly revenue growth eased to 13.5% in September from 20% cumulatively, while expenditure growth accelerated to 8.6% from 7.1%, calculations from the Ministry’s data show.

The primary balance, which excludes interest payments and is the central indicator under Sri Lanka’s IMF-supported program, posted a surplus of Rs. 1,843.9 billion, up 25.8% from Rs. 1,465.1 billion, and already 5.1 times the Rs. 360 billion primary surplus projected for the full year in the 2026 Budget. September’s primary surplus of about Rs. 199.3 billion, against an implied interest bill of about Rs. 212 billion, was the only factor keeping the overall balance positive.

The Budget projects an annual overall deficit of Rs. 2,257 billion, implying the final quarter must absorb a deficit of about Rs. 2,279 billion to meet the target.

Tax revenue rose 19.3% to Rs. 4,252.1 billion, with VAT up 22% to Rs. 1,505.6 billion and income tax up 20% to Rs. 996.4 billion. VAT on imports, the largest single component collected by Sri Lanka Customs, rose 14% to Rs. 690.3 billion, while Customs excise duty rose 15% to Rs. 636.1 billion. Motor vehicle excise accounted for Rs. 381.0 billion of that, up 9.1% or Rs. 31.7 billion, and excise on liquor rose 22% to Rs. 204.9 billion.

The Ministry identified vehicle imports as the principal source of growth. “The total revenue (excluding grants) increased by 20 percent to Rs. 4,594.9 billion in the first nine months of 2026 from Rs. 3,827.0 billion in the same period of 2025, mainly due to the substantial revenue collection from import of motor vehicles,” it said.

Non-tax revenue rose 29.8% to Rs. 342.9 billion, or 95.2% of its annual estimate, while grants fell 14.6% to Rs. 6.7 billion.

Customs collected 89.8% of its Rs. 2,206 billion annual estimate, the Inland Revenue Department 83.9% of Rs. 2,401 billion and the Excise Department 84.2% of Rs. 245 billion, taking the combined achievement to 86.6%. “In the first nine months of 2026, Sri Lanka Customs and Inland Revenue department became the largest contributors to the Government Revenue, individually accounting for 47 percent of the total tax revenue collected, while Excise Department was the third-largest contributor,” the Ministry said.

Recurrent expenditure rose 5.6% to Rs. 4,036.6 billion, or 69.1% of the annual estimate, with interest at 45% of the total, subsidies and transfers 26% and salaries and wages 23%. Interest payments fell 5% to Rs. 1,821.6 billion.

Capital expenditure and net lending rose 19.2% to Rs. 542.8 billion, but reached only 31.6% of the Rs. 1,719 billion allocation, leaving more than two thirds of planned investment spending unexecuted with a quarter of the year remaining. The IMF has pressed the Government to accelerate spending execution, including on disaster-related support.

The economy expanded 4.2% in the second quarter of 2026, slowing from 5.0% a year earlier, with gross domestic product at constant prices of Rs. 3,029.8 billion against Rs. 2,908.6 billion.

title: Shanghai Power Transmission and Distribution to power transmission network | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 10 November 2026 00:52
-     - 13

The National Transmission Network Service Provider Ltd., (NTNSP) and Shanghai Electric Power Transmission and Distribution Engineering Co., Ltd., part of China’s Shanghai Electric Group, signed an engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contract to expand Sri Lanka’s electricity transmission network. 

Sri Lankan engineering firm ComCorp Ltd., will serve as the local engineering partner to Shanghai Power Transmission and Distribution Co. Ltd. (SPTDE), a subsidiary of the renowned Shanghai Electric Group of China, which is the EPC contractor for the 87.7 km high-voltage transmission line project for NTNSP.

The contract covers Package 2 of the Asian Development Bank-funded Power System Strengthening and Renewable Energy Integration Project (PSSREIP). The scope comprises the construction of a 78 km, 132 kV Matara - Hambantota transmission line, a 7.7 km double-circuit in-and-out connection to Homagama Grid Substation from the existing Horana -Padukka 132 kV transmission line, a 1.5 km single-circuit in-and-out connection to Mirigama Grid Substation from the existing New Habarana - Veyangoda 220 kV transmission line, and a 0.5 km in-and-out connection to Negombo Grid Substation from the existing Katunayake - Bolawatta 132 kV transmission line.

The new lines and connections are expected to increase the amount of electricity the network can carry and improve the reliability of supply. The work forms part of a wider effort to prepare Sri Lanka’s grid for more wind and solar generation. As new generation comes online, expanding the transmission network helps carry electricity from where it is produced to where households and businesses need it.

The contract, finalised 5 November, builds on Shanghai Electric’s previous work in Sri Lanka, which includes the 220 kV Veyangoda Grid Substation, the 220/132 kV New Chilaw Grid Substation and a two-bay extension at the New Anuradhapura Grid Substation. The company has also worked on 220 kV transmission infrastructure associated with the Norochcholai Power Plant. Its international portfolio includes high-voltage transmission and substation projects in Malaysia, Indonesia, Pakistan, the Maldives and Myanmar, with capabilities spanning engineering, procurement, construction and commissioning.

ComCorp’s work with electricity utilities dates back to 1997, when it was established in Sri Lanka as a licensed office of Belgium’s Electronic Instruments International (EII). The company began by introducing Digital Fault and Disturbance Recording technology to utilities in the region (Thailand, Malaysia, Bangladesh, UAE, Indonesia, Sudan, Algeria...etc.)These systems capture what happens when a fault occurs, giving utility engineers the data they need to investigate disruptions. Today, ComCorp remains a leading provider of power system monitoring and disturbance recording solutions, backed by three decades of experience and an established presence in the electricity utility sector.

Over the years, ComCorp has expanded into power transmission and distribution, protection and control systems, power transformers, engineering consultancy and utility asset management. Its services include equipment supply, installation, testing and commissioning, as well as turnkey project delivery. The company has worked directly together with over 15 Utilities and international technology and engineering firms including LEM, Qualitrol and many other EPC’s around the globe.

The project pairs Shanghai Electric’s experience delivering high-voltage infrastructure internationally with ComCorp’s experience coordinating engineering work in Sri Lanka. That local experience is relevant to a package that spans a long-distance transmission corridor in the south and three separate grid connections. For ComCorp, the appointment builds on its work with international engineering companies serving electricity utilities in Sri Lanka and the region.

NTNSP Chairman Nusith Kumaratunga and Chief Executive Officer Eng. N. S. Wettasinghe attended the signing alongside Director of Design Eng. Anuruddha Thilakarathna, Project Director Eng. S. W. Kumarawadu and Project Manager Eng. R. Jeewagan. Other senior NTNSP officials and engineers were present, together with representatives of SPTDE and ComCorp.

title: Govt. to cut detention period to 48 hours, withdraw key clauses  in Organised Crimes Bill | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 10 November 2026 00:51
-     - 7

The Government has agreed to reduce the maximum detention period under the proposed Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill from 72 to 48 hours and withdraw several contentious provisions, following constitutional challenges before the Supreme Court.

The Attorney General’s office informed the Court yesterday (9) that the proposed amendments would also remove provisions relating to tattoos and body marks, offences under the Excise Ordinance and prior court approval for publishing information on cases involving serious crimes.

The Government also intends to amend copyright-related provisions under the Intellectual Property Act and is considering further changes to clauses governing detention orders and the Bail Act following discussions with policymakers.

The amendments are expected to be presented during the Committee Stage of the Bill in Parliament. A document outlining the proposed changes was submitted to the Supreme Court and lawyers representing the petitioners.

The submissions were made as a three-member Supreme Court bench comprising Chief Justice Preethi Padman Surasena and Justices Achala Wengappuli and Sampath Abeykoon resumed hearing 26 petitions challenging the constitutionality of the proposed legislation.

The petitions, filed by several parties, including the Bar Association of Sri Lanka, contend that certain provisions of the Bill, published in the Gazette on 6 October, are inconsistent with the Constitution.

The latest amendments follow President Anura Kumara Dissanayake’s announcement that the Government would not proceed with the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill or the proposed Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill without broader consultations with the public and relevant stakeholders.

Addressing the National Trade Union Conference on Saturday (7), the President said the Government would engage civil society organisations and other concerned parties to build consensus before proceeding with the legislation.

IFC will help HNB develop scalable supply chain finance solutions connecting its corporate clients with suppliers and distributors. By combining HNB’s deep understanding of the local market and longstanding relationships across the corporate, SME and microenterprise sectors with IFC’s international expertise, we aim to develop scalable supply chain finance solutions that improve access to working capital, strengthen business linkages and support sustainable growth. IFC Regional Vice President for Asia and the Pacific Sarvesh Suri said: “SMEs are the foundation of Sri Lanka’s economy, and their growth is critical for creating jobs, building stronger local supply chains and driving sustainable growth. title: CoPF calls for independent fuel pricing regulator | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 10 November 2026 00:50
-     - 7

The Parliamentary Committee on Public Finance (CoPF) has called for an independent regulatory mechanism to ensure transparency in fuel pricing and fair competition between the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation (CPC) and private fuel suppliers.

The issue was raised at a committee meeting chaired by SJB MP Dr. Harsha de Silva, where members examined differences in fuel landing costs between the State-owned CPC and private importers.

Officials told the committee that the CPC meets part of domestic demand through its refinery, while private suppliers import all their refined petroleum products. Despite differences in import costs, private operators are required to price fuel based on rates announced by the CPC.

The committee expressed concern that the arrangement could create competitive distortions and called for a transparent pricing mechanism that takes account of import costs, taxes and distribution expenses.

Members also stressed the need to replace blanket fuel subsidies with targeted assistance for low-income communities and the public transport sector.

The meeting also examined proposed standards for imported vehicle tyres and changes to the Aswesuma welfare benefits programme.

The committee reviewed regulations issued under the Imports and Exports (Control) Act through Extraordinary Gazette No. 2508/27 dated October 1, 2026, and Supplementary Estimate No. 07 of 2026.

title: Banking sector credit-to-deposit ratio tops 70% for first time in three years | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 10 November 2026 00:49
-     - 8

Sri Lanka’s banking sector Credit-to-Deposit Ratio (CDR) has exceeded 70% for the first time in three years, reaching 74.0% by end June 2026 and surpassing its long-term average, with the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) flagging credit growth outpacing deposits and a widening credit gap as potential sources of systemic risk.

In its recent Financial Stability Review 2026, the CBSL said financial intermediation, the channelling of deposits into loans by banks, strengthened during the review period on the back of continued credit expansion. The CDR, which maintained the upward momentum that emerged in early 2025, rose from 63.9% at end 2024 and 69.9% at end 2025.

Banking sector credit grew 23.6% year-on-year at end Q2 of 2026, more than double the 11.4% recorded a year earlier, while retail funding, comprising demand, savings and term deposits, increased by only 6.7%. The CBSL said credit accelerated markedly amid the continued economic recovery and the accommodative monetary conditions that prevailed during much of the period, while deposit growth remained comparatively moderate. Notably, the rise in the CDR occurred alongside broadly stable GDP growth, suggesting that the recovery in credit demand outpaced changes in overall economic activity.

Even so, the CDR remained below pre-crisis levels, having stood at 82.7% at end 2021, indicating that the increase partly reflected the normalisation of financial intermediation from the exceptionally subdued levels recorded during 2023 and 2024.

However, a sustained widening of the gap between credit and deposit growth could increase funding pressures and contribute to a gradual erosion of liquidity buffers if credit expansion continued to significantly outpace growth in stable deposit funding, the CBSL warned. That erosion is already visible: the banking sector’s Rupee Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), which measures high quality liquid assets against 30-day net cash outflows, fell to 272.5% at end Q2 of 2026 from 328.5% a year earlier, while the share of high quality liquid assets in total assets declined to 29.5% from 33.8% at end 2025. The CBSL attributed the decline mainly to banks shifting assets from Government securities to private sector lending, though liquidity ratios remained well above regulatory thresholds.

The private sector credit cycle continued to progress within the expansionary phase, with the private sector credit-to-GDP ratio rising throughout the period. Consumption loans, the banking sector’s largest credit segment, grew 29.1% year-on-year at end Q2 of 2026, against 11.0% a year earlier, driven by pawning facilities, which rose 49.2%, and personal loans, which grew 21.3%, including loans for vehicle purchases. The CBSL attributed the surge in pawning to rising gold prices, warning of market and collateral risks should global gold prices correct sharply.

Across the financial sector, comprising banks and finance companies (FCs), motor vehicle related credit rose to 12.9% of total credit by end June 2026 from 9.8% at end 2024, following the relaxation of vehicle import restrictions in early 2025. Gold-backed lending rose to 12.0% from 9.8% over the same period. Total credit extended by banks and FCs accelerated from 14.0% year-on-year in June 2025 to a peak of 27.9% in March 2026, before easing marginally to 26.4% by June 2026.

At the same time, the Credit Gap, which measures how far credit deviates from its long-term trend relative to GDP, remained in positive territory and widened further. While a positive gap was consistent with the recovery in lending after the prolonged contraction of 2022 to 2024, its continued widening alongside rapid private sector credit growth warranted close monitoring, the CBSL said. A sustained expansion significantly above trend could lead to a buildup of borrower leverage, increased risk-taking and sectoral credit concentrations if not matched by growth in borrowers’ income and repayment capacity. Six sectors accounted for 72.9% of banking sector credit at end Q2 of 2026, up from 71.1% a year earlier.

In response, the CBSL raised the Overnight Policy Rate (OPR) by 100 basis points to 8.75% on 26 May 2026, its first policy rate increase since June 2023. It also tightened loan-to-value (LTV) limits, which cap the size of a loan relative to the value of the asset financed. In two rounds, in November 2025 and May 2026, the maximum LTV for new commercial vehicles was cut from 80% to 60% and for other new vehicles to 40%, while the limit for used vehicles was lowered from 70% to 60%. A maximum LTV of 70% on gold-backed credit took effect on 25 May 2026, alongside tighter risk weights. As these measures transmit with a lag, their impact on the pace and composition of credit growth would require continued monitoring, the CBSL said.

Meanwhile, the CBSL’s Credit Supply Survey showed loan demand continued to strengthen in Q2 of 2026 across the retail, corporate, SME and state-owned enterprise (SOE) sectors, although at a more moderate pace than in Q1. The expansion was largely supported by higher working capital requirements, demand for short-term loans and a revival of investment activity.

Banks expected both lending activity and credit demand to remain positive in Q3 of 2026. However, their willingness to lend is expected to increase at a slower pace, reflecting a more cautious outlook amid anticipated inflationary pressures, rising operating costs, exchange rate volatility and geopolitical uncertainties.

title: India–Sri Lanka economic ties spotlights inaugural Colombo Port City Investor Forum in India | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 10 November 2026 00:33
-     - 11

Colombo Port City Economic Commission Chairman Harsha Amarasekera, PC

Deputy High Commissioner 

of Sri Lanka for Southern India Dr. Ganesanathan Geathiswaran

CHEC Port City Colombo 

Deputy Managing Director 

Thulci Aluwihare

Building on the longstanding economic relationship between India and Sri Lanka, the Colombo Port City Investor Forum, held at the Hyatt Regency, Chennai, on 4 November, explored new avenues for investment, enterprise and cross-border business partnerships. 

Hosted by the Deputy High Commission of Sri Lanka in Chennai, in collaboration with Port City Colombo (PCC), the forum brought together over 200 participants, including business leaders from the real estate, financial services, logistics, IT and technology sectors, representatives of leading Indian industry chambers, investors and policymakers, to explore how closer commercial engagement can create opportunities for businesses in both countries. The invitation-only forum marked Port City Colombo’s first investor forum in India, underscoring its commitment to deepening engagement with the Indian business and investment community and translating longstanding bilateral economic ties into tangible business opportunities.

The program opened with an address by Deputy High Commissioner of Sri Lanka for Southern India Dr. Ganesanathan Geathiswaran. “India and Sri Lanka are bound by geography, history and commerce, and that relationship is stronger than ever. There is considerable scope to deepen these ties through greater business engagement and investment. Chennai, with its strong industrial base and entrepreneurial ecosystem, is an important market for this conversation. We hope the forum will help build lasting partnerships between businesses in our two countries and translate shared opportunities into meaningful economic outcomes,” he said.

A central theme of the forum was “India’s Growth Story, Strengthened: Why Sri Lanka, Why Now”, enabling Indian businesses to extend their capabilities and market reach without moving away from their domestic base. Sri Lanka’s proximity to India, shared time zone, cultural similarities and established commercial and legal institutions offer practical advantages for businesses seeking to serve regional and international markets. Discussions explored opportunities across real estate, product engineering, treasury, data analytics, cybersecurity and business process operations, alongside data centres, technology, AI and other emerging areas. The discussions also examined how investment facilitation and a predictable regulatory environment could support businesses evaluating Sri Lanka as part of their regional expansion strategies.

“For investors, the strength of a proposition lies not just in the opportunity it offers, but in the certainty of the framework within which they operate. Port City Colombo has been designed to provide that clarity through a statutory framework and defined investor safeguards. For Indian businesses looking to grow their reach, Sri Lanka offers proximity, familiarity and access to wider regional opportunities. This is about extending business capabilities and reaching new markets as a complementary partner, with the centre of growth remaining in India,” said Colombo Port City Economic Commission Chairman Harsha Amarasekera, PC. He further emphasised that Port City Colombo is a project of national importance, operating under the direct purview of the Office of Sri Lanka’s President, Anura Kumara Dissanayake, who also serves as Finance Minister, underscoring the Government’s interest in the project.

CHEC Port City Colombo Ltd., Deputy Managing Director Thulci Aluwihare outlined Port City Colombo’s proposition as an international business and investment destination, highlighting its position as Sri Lanka’s only foreign currency-designated Special Economic Zone. He also detailed the statutory framework underpinning the zone, which includes a single-window approval process, investor safeguards, a stabilisation mechanism, international arbitration provisions, 100% foreign ownership and the ability to transact in 16 foreign currencies, including the Indian rupee. 

A panel discussion brought together TVS Vehicle Mobility Solutions CEO and CII SR Taskforce on International Business Development Co-Chairman Madhu Raghunath, JLL Senior Director and Head – Centre of Excellence, Strategic Consulting and Value & Risk Advisory, India & Sri Lanka Robin S., Amarasekera and Aluwihare to discuss sectoral opportunities, regulatory facilitation and prospects for business partnerships.

Robin S., said: “For Indian businesses exploring opportunities beyond the domestic market, geographic proximity, ease of doing business and access to new growth markets are important considerations. A clear regulatory framework and transparent incentive framework give Port City Colombo the ingredients for serious interest from India, and the conversations thus far show that interest is building.”

The Investor Forum in Chennai marks an important step in Port City Colombo’s efforts to deepen engagement with the Indian business and investment community. Going forward, continued dialogue will be pursued to further potential cross-border partnerships and unlocking new avenues for investment and collaboration.

title: National Christian Council raises concerns over anti-terrorism, organised crime and NGO Bills | Daily FT

The National Christian Council of Sri Lanka (NCCSL) has issued a statement raising concerns over the proposed Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill (PSTA), Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill (POCB), and Non-Governmental Organisations (Registration and Supervision) Bill.

NCCSL said it believes that the rule of law must remain central to all efforts to maintain public security and respond to corruption. The Christian faith affirms the inherent worth and dignity of every human person, calling us to stand for a society where justice is administered fairly, public institutions remain accountable, and no individual is deprived of fundamental rights through arbitrary State action. The statement follows:

Affirming the positives

Raising severe dangers and concerns

Despite these steps, a rigorous evaluation of the proposed package of Bills - comprising the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill (PSTA), Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill (POCB), and Non-Governmental Organisations (Registration and Supervision) Bill - reveals alarming dangers:

1. Overbroad definitions and protecting State over people: The PSTA shifts focus from protecting civilians to protecting State institutions against dissent. Defining terrorism and serious crime through vague criteria like “unduly compelling a Government” or considering dress, tattoos, and associations risks criminalising identity and peaceful protests.

2. Erosion of judicial oversight and executive overreach: Extraordinary detention powers up to 12 months are vested in executive officials, such as the Defence Secretary or senior police, rather than judicial officers. Magistrates are stripped of discretion, compelled to give effect to executive orders without granting bail. Furthermore, critical bail safeguards agreed upon by advisory committees were secretly removed from the tabled PSTA text. Suspects face cumulative custody extending up to three years.

3. Expanded military powers and digital surveillance: The PSTA expands warrantless arrest powers to armed forces and coast guard personnel, while restricting suspect legal counsel through subordinate circulars. Concurrently, the POCB permits intrusive digital surveillance, device decryption, and subscriber data extraction without court orders.

4. Suppression of civil society under the NGO Bill: The NGO Bill mandates prior authorisation, penalises unregistered operations with fines up to Rs. 1 million, enforces warrantless property inspections, and requires NGOs to align with Government policy. This crosses the line from regulation to control, which is contrary to human rights norms. Contrary to Government claims, UN experts and research establish that these blanket restrictions contradict FATF Recommendation 8’s risk-based approach.

5. Cumulative impact and lack of consultation: Together, these laws form a mutually reinforcing architecture of suppression drafted without transparent, inclusive consultation with relevant stakeholders and civil society including religious bodies.

Conclusion and call to action

Legislation dealing with national security or corruption must never suppress dissent or dismantle democratic accountability. We call upon the Government of Sri Lanka to immediately withdraw or substantially overhaul these draft bills. True national security and good governance are achieved when human dignity is protected, equality before the law is guaranteed for all and the State wields its power with accountability and in accordance with the Constitution.

title: Budget 2027: Beyond promises to real progress | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 10 November 2026 00:40
-     - 10

Why better incomes, productive investment, effective public administration and responsible spending must become the measures of economic progress

Sri Lanka’s 2027 Budget Speech is scheduled for 12 November 2026. After years of economic hardship, public expectations are understandably high. Families want relief from living costs, better employment, reliable public services and greater confidence in the future.

Discussion has focused particularly on public sector salary increases. Fair remuneration matters, but a more fundamental question must guide the Budget debate: Will the government’s decisions produce lasting improvements in people’s lives?

Since the 2022 crisis, Sri Lanka has restored a measure of stability. Growth has resumed, foreign exchange reserves have improved and public financial management has strengthened. According to the World Bank, the economy grew by 4.7% during the first half of 2026. Yet recovery in national statistics does not automatically translate into recovery for households.

The 2027 Budget should therefore be judged less by the size of its promises than by its capacity to increase real incomes, expand productive employment, attract investment and turn public resources into measurable results.

Salary increases must improve real incomes

Public servants have faced considerable financial pressure, and higher salaries can provide welcome relief. But the increase expected in 2027 largely completes the three-stage salary revision announced in the 2025 Budget, rather than constituting an entirely new initiative.

It is also important to distinguish between nominal wages—the money an employee receives—and real wages—what that money can purchase. If a worker earning Rs. 60,000 receives an additional Rs. 5,000, the nominal increase is about 8.3%. But if prices have risen by roughly 8% over the same period, the gain in purchasing power is small.

Households do not evaluate prosperity from salary slips alone. They assess whether earnings can meet the costs of food, transport, electricity, housing, education and healthcare.

Regular salary reviews are justified, but they must be financially sustainable and accompanied by efforts to improve productivity, contain living costs and raise earnings across the economy. The objective should be better living standards, not merely higher figures on payrolls.

Recovery has not reached every household

Despite the improvement in headline indicators, many Sri Lankans remain under financial strain. The Colombo Consumer Price Index recorded annual inflation of 8.3% in October 2026. The World Bank estimated poverty at 16.9% in 2025. Although overall unemployment stood at 4% in the second quarter of 2026, unemployment among people aged 15–24 was 17.8%, while labour force participation was only 50%.

The Health Ministry’s 2025 Nutrition Month data also reported that 16.1% of children under five were underweight. These indicators remind us that economic hardship cannot be measured by GDP growth alone. Poverty, weak labour market participation and poor nutrition are not isolated social concerns: they reduce human potential and ultimately weaken the economy’s productive capacity. Policies should therefore be evaluated for their effects on employment, opportunity and the distribution of gains, not growth alone.

Another distinction is often overlooked: lower inflation does not necessarily mean lower prices. If a food item rises from Rs. 100 to Rs. 200, a subsequent slowdown in inflation may simply mean that it becomes more expensive at a slower rate. Families still have to pay the higher price.

For pensioners, low-income households, informal workers and unemployed young people, recovery will feel incomplete until purchasing power and economic security improve. Budget policy must therefore combine stability with targeted support and opportunities to earn sustainable incomes.

Build an economy that produces, exports and employs

Sri Lanka cannot sustainably improve living standards through salary increases, subsidies and tax concessions alone. Those measures depend ultimately on the country’s capacity to produce more goods and services, generate income and collect revenue without creating renewed fiscal instability.

Agriculture, manufacturing, tourism, technology and export-oriented services all offer potential. Small and medium-sized enterprises are especially important because they create jobs and economic activity throughout the country. Yet, many struggle with expensive finance, outdated equipment, limited market access and cumbersome administrative procedures.

Farmers need reliable irrigation, storage, transport and opportunities to add value to what they grow. Entrepreneurs need accessible finance, skilled workers and predictable rules. Exporters need productive infrastructure and efficient trade procedures.

A stronger productive economy also depends on improving the quality of employment. Young Sri Lankans need pathways from education and training into rewarding work. This requires practical cooperation among universities, technical institutes, employers and regional businesses. Supporting enterprise outside Colombo would help distribute opportunities more fairly and reduce the pressure on young people to seek their future abroad.

Foreign exchange earnings deserve particular emphasis. Borrowing dollars is not the same as earning dollars. Loans can temporarily meet financing needs, but they bring repayment obligations. Sustainable foreign exchange comes from competitive exports, tourism, services and other productive activities, supported by formal workers’ remittances.

A credible national strategy should connect investment in skills and infrastructure with measurable targets for production, exports and employment. Announcements without sustained implementation will not build a competitive economy.

Restore confidence for domestic and foreign investors

Investment brings employment, technology, tax revenue and opportunities for growth. But investors commit capital when they believe policies will remain reasonably predictable and institutions will treat them fairly.

Sri Lanka must address delays in approvals, uncertainty over contracts, abrupt policy changes and inconsistent application of regulations. Existing investors also require timely, transparent remedies when legitimate concerns arise. Their experiences influence the decisions of potential new investors.

Investment promotion should consequently be judged by projects that actually begin operations, jobs created and exports generated—not only by investment pledges or memoranda of understanding. A transparent, time-bound approval system, with clear channels for resolving disputes, could make a substantial difference. Equally important is consistent treatment of domestic enterprises, which are often the starting point for sustainable expansion.

The Government must, of course, investigate corruption and hold wrongdoers accountable. Strong institutions and the rule of law are essential to confidence. Yet public communication should also convey a positive economic direction: where investment opportunities lie, how obstacles will be removed and what policies businesses can reasonably expect.

Accountability and investment promotion should reinforce rather than undermine one another. A credible government can investigate past misconduct while providing lawful, consistent and efficient conditions for future investment.

Make public administration accountable and capable of acting

Even well-designed policies will fail if public institutions cannot implement them. Salary improvements alone cannot create an effective civil service. Officials also need professional training, modern systems, clear responsibilities and the authority to make timely decisions.

There is concern that some officials hesitate to approve contracts, procurement decisions or projects because they fear later investigations. Such caution can delay development and discourage investors. But weakening anti-corruption institutions is not the answer.

The proper response is to establish clear procedures, transparent procurement standards, reliable documentation and fair review mechanisms. Deliberate misconduct must be investigated and punished. Officials acting honestly, reasonably and within the law should receive appropriate procedural protections.

Political leaders and administrators must share responsibility for removing unnecessary complexity and improving coordination across agencies. Good governance means decisions that are both accountable and timely—not the absence of decisions.

The public should not have to navigate overlapping offices to obtain routine approvals. Simplified procedures, better digital services and clearly assigned responsibilities would improve the experience of citizens as well as businesses. Administrative reform is therefore not a separate concern from economic policy. It is one of the conditions for translating policy into results.

Balance development, inflation

and taxation

Public investment in transport, energy, irrigation, education and healthcare can reduce business costs and expand opportunity. However, every major project should be assessed for economic benefits, financial affordability, environmental effects and long-term maintenance needs. Large expenditure is not, by itself, evidence of development.

Price stability also requires sound monetary and fiscal policies, dependable supplies and competitive markets. A reasonably stable exchange rate helps households and firms plan, but an artificially strong rupee could damage export competitiveness. Durable currency stability depends on productivity, foreign exchange earnings, adequate reserves and confidence.

Tax relief is understandably popular after years of hardship. Nevertheless, broad reductions without alternative revenue could weaken public finances and threaten recovery. A better approach is to widen compliance, reduce evasion, improve administration, limit waste and offer carefully targeted relief when affordable.

The Budget must confront these trade-offs directly. Social protection and economic development are both necessary, but they must be financed within a credible fiscal framework.

This means choosing among competing priorities rather than pretending all demands can be met immediately. Protecting essential healthcare and education, maintaining productive infrastructure and providing well-targeted assistance may yield greater benefits than highly visible but poorly prepared projects. Responsible budgeting is ultimately a question of priorities as much as accounting.

Close the gap between Budget allocations and delivery

Perhaps the clearest test of the 2027 Budget is whether allocated development funds become completed projects.

During the first half of 2026, approximately Rs. 1,719 billion was allocated for capital expenditure and net lending for the full year, but only about Rs. 280 billion had been spent by the end of June—just 16.3%. By comparison, total government expenditure had reached 39.2% of annual allocations and recurrent expenditure 45.9%. The comparable first-half capital expenditure and net lending rate in 2025 was 17.5%.

These numbers do not establish that the whole year will end poorly. Construction and procurement payments are often concentrated later in the year. Nor is every unspent rupee evidence of failure. Still, such low first-half implementation rates deserve careful investigation.

Delayed expenditure has consequences beyond financial statements. If a hospital project stalls, patients wait for services. If a school building remains incomplete, students lose learning opportunities. Delayed irrigation systems affect farm output, while unfinished roads prolong transport costs.

Postponed projects also reduce demand for construction workers, materials, machinery, transport and local suppliers. Thus, implementation failures can weaken both immediate economic activity and long-term productivity.

The causes are varied: inadequate preparation, land acquisition problems, procurement delays, environmental approvals, weak interagency coordination, shortages of technical expertise and difficulties releasing funds. Uncertainty among decision-makers may also contribute. No single official or institution can reasonably bear all the blame.

A serious response must examine the complete project cycle—from selection and preparation to procurement, funding, execution and evaluation—rather than merely calling for faster spending.

Projects should enter the Budget only when their feasibility, land requirements, approvals and implementation responsibilities are sufficiently clear. Otherwise, the government creates unrealistic expectations and later confronts predictable delays. Treasury funding plans and implementing agencies’ work schedules also need to be aligned from the outset. More disciplined preparation could prevent many delays before they arise.

Measure results, not just money spent

Spending an allocation before year-end is not necessarily good management. Rushed purchases, weak construction and unnecessary projects can waste public money. Equally, lower spending may sometimes reflect cost savings or sensible cancellation of unnecessary activities.

The central question is not how much the government spends, but what that spending achieves.

This is the value of performance-based budgeting. A road project should be assessed not only by its construction cost but by whether it reduces travel time, improves access to markets and benefits nearby communities. A hospital investment should be evaluated through service quality and patient access. Irrigation spending should be linked to agricultural productivity and farmers’ incomes.

Every major publicly funded project should have a realistic timetable, a responsible institution, published financial and physical milestones, and measurable intended benefits. Quarterly progress reports should show what has been completed as well as what has been paid.

Projects falling behind schedule need early diagnosis and corrective action. Officials should be held accountable for performance while receiving the resources, training and lawful protections needed to do their jobs. Government should also prioritise completing worthwhile existing projects before multiplying new announcements.

Independent evaluation has a role here. Citizens deserve to know not only whether a project was completed, but whether its promised benefits materialised. Publishing straightforward evaluations would help policymakers learn from mistakes, improve future project selection and strengthen public trust. The aim should be improvement, not simply assigning blame when targets are missed.

At year-end, citizens should be able to ask a simple question: What tangible improvements resulted from the funds Parliament approved? If there is no convincing answer, impressive Budget figures offer little comfort.

What the 2027 Budget should deliver

The Budget should combine immediate relief with a credible plan for future prosperity. Public sector salary commitments and targeted assistance matter, but they should not overshadow private sector workers, self-employed people, farmers, pensioners, small businesses and unemployed youth.

The Government should explain how it will strengthen production, create productive jobs, expand exports, encourage domestic and foreign investment and improve essential services. Each priority needs a realistic target, adequate financing, a responsible agency and a public timetable.

This also requires an honest account of fiscal limits. Sri Lanka remains constrained by debt obligations and available revenue. Ambitious promises that cannot be funded or implemented may endanger hard-won stability.

Above all, ministries should be judged by outcomes, not the number of projects they announce. Parliament and the public need accessible information on costs, progress, delays and results. Transparency should support practical problem-solving rather than become another reporting exercise.

A useful Budget should also distinguish clearly between measures that provide immediate relief and reforms whose benefits will emerge over several years. People can accept difficult choices more readily when the government explains the purpose, likely timing and costs of its decisions. This requires honest communication and consistent follow-through, not merely ambitious language on Budget day.

Conclusion: Turn recovery into real improvement

Sri Lanka has made important progress since the 2022 economic crisis. But stability and growth are only the foundation. The deeper test is whether families can afford essential needs, young people can find meaningful work, businesses can invest confidently and public services deliver reliably.

These goals demand a more productive and export-oriented economy, responsible fiscal management, investor confidence and public administration that combines integrity with the ability to act.

The 2027 Budget should mark a shift from promises to implementation, from allocations to outcomes, and from short-term relief to lasting prosperity.

This is not simply a matter of political criticism. It is a constructive test of economic leadership. Ultimately, the success of a national Budget should be measured not by the promises made in Parliament, but by the improvements people experience in their everyday lives.

title: Budget 2027: Will Sri Lanka remain a tea plantation economy or become global capital of tea? | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 10 November 2026 00:10
-     - 13

A defining economic choice

As Sri Lanka prepares for the National Budget on 12 November, the country faces a defining economic question. How do we generate the foreign exchange, investment and jobs needed to accelerate growth in an increasingly competitive global economy? For decades, tea has been one of Sri Lanka’s most celebrated exports. Ceylon Tea remains one of the few truly global brands the country can proudly claim as its own. Yet while we continue to grow and export some of the world’s finest tea, much of the industry’s most profitable activities are happening elsewhere. The issue is no longer about producing better tea. The issue is whether Sri Lanka can capture more revenue share from the global value added tea business itself.

A success story that has reached its limits

The tea industry deserves enormous credit for its contribution to the national economy even though things have been rough due the political turmoil/ war in the Middle East. During the first nine months of 2026, tea exports generated approximately $ 1.083 billion, compared with $ 1.163 billion during the corresponding period in 2025. Export volumes have declined by 4%, falling from 198.3 million kilograms to 189.4 million kilograms.

While export earnings in Sri Lankan Rupees increased slightly from Rs. 347 billion to Rs. 350 billion, this improvement was largely driven by currency depreciation rather than stronger export performance. These figures reveal an important reality. Sri Lanka is earning less in foreign currency while exporting less tea. At a time when the country urgently needs foreign exchange, that trend should concern policymakers. This is not a criticism of the tea industry. Rather, it is recognition that the global tea business has fundamentally changed.

Where the real money is being made

Around the world, the highest profits in most industries are rarely captured by producers of raw materials. The greatest value is created through innovation, branding, packaging, logistics, retailing, customer ownership and global distribution networks. Tea is no exception. A striking statistic is that only 50% of Sri Lanka’s tea exports are currently sold as value-added products such as tea bags, packets and instant tea. While the value addition is commendable progress even though it’s half the total volumes exported, it also highlights how much more value can still be captured through advanced blending, product development, wellness beverages, digital trading and international brand ownership. Globally, the retail value of tea products is many times greater than the export value earned by producing nations. Simply put, producing the tea leaf is no longer where the greatest wealth is created.

The warning signals from global markets

Market dynamics are changing rapidly. Exports to Iraq, traditionally one of Sri Lanka’s largest tea destinations, declined sharply from 30 million kilograms to 18.4 million kilograms, a reduction of almost 39%. Shipments to Libya fell from 15.9 million kilograms to 6.6 million kilograms, representing a decline of nearly 60%. Exports to China, one of the world’s largest consumer markets, declined by 10% to 7.1 million kilograms. Even Chile, a strong growth story in recent years, saw imports of Sri Lankan tea decline from 8.5 million kilograms to 6.3 million kilograms. Although exports to Türkiye increased dramatically by 134%, rising from 15.2 million kilograms to 35.7 million kilograms, much of this reflects changing regional trade routes and geopolitical circumstances rather than long-term structural growth. The lesson is clear. Overdependence on a limited number of markets is becoming increasingly risky.

The Russian lesson Sri Lanka cannot ignore

The Russian market offers an important lesson in strategic value creation. For years, Russia imported tea from producing countries and gradually developed domestic blending, packaging and distribution capabilities. Import policies encouraged local processing while international producers continued supplying bulk tea. The result was predictable. Tea-producing countries continued to export raw material, but much of the value creation, employment generation, branding and profitability migrated to Russia itself. From a Russian perspective, this was sound economic policy. From Sri Lanka’s perspective, it exposed a structural vulnerability. We continue to produce some of the world’s finest tea, but others are becoming increasingly successful at capturing the value created after the tea leaves leave our shores.

The three strategic choices

Sri Lanka effectively has three options. Option One: Defend the Current Model. We can continue investing heavily in promoting Pure Ceylon Tea and strengthening its premium image. This remains essential. The Lion Logo is one of Sri Lanka’s most valuable national assets and must be protected at all costs. However, branding alone is unlikely to transform the sector from its current $ 1 billion export base into the multi-billion-dollar growth engine that the economy requires.

Option Two: Pursue Better Market Access. Sri Lanka can continue negotiating trade agreements and seeking improved access for value-added exports. While worthwhile, many countries are unlikely to dismantle policies that support their own packaging and blending industries. Trade diplomacy should continue, but it is unlikely to become the breakthrough solution. 

Option Three: Build a Sri Lankan Tea Hub. This is the boldest option and potentially the most transformative. Under a Tea Hub framework, Sri Lanka would allow the controlled importation of teas from other origins into a highly regulated Free Trade Zone. These teas could then be blended, processed, packaged and re-exported from Sri Lanka. The country would evolve from being primarily a tea producer to becoming a tea business centre. That distinction could redefine the future of the industry. Should this be part of the reform agenda that Budget 2027 should address is the million dollar question. In fact this has been the battle ground at many pre-Budget debates in the tea industry.

The fear that cannot be ignored

The biggest concern surrounding a Tea Hub is obvious. Will it damage the Ceylon Tea brand? The answer depends entirely on how the strategy is designed. These concerns are legitimate and deserve serious consideration. However, protecting Pure Ceylon Tea and developing a Tea Hub need not be mutually exclusive goals. The solution is a clear dual-brand architecture. Tier One: Pure Ceylon Tea-100% Sri Lankan origin, Lion Logo protected, Existing Tea Board standards maintained and Premium positioning preserved.

Tier Two: Sri Lanka Tea Hub Certified- Internationally blended products, Separate certification system, Full digital traceability and Distinct visual identity Consumers would know exactly what they are purchasing. The national brand would remain protected while a second engine of growth is created.

Why Budget 2027 must be the turning point

Budget 2027 presents a rare opportunity to think bigger about tea. Instead of viewing the industry as an agricultural sector requiring periodic support, Sri Lanka should position tea as a national export competitiveness strategy. A dedicated Sri Lanka Tea Hub Authority should be established to coordinate policy, investment promotion and governance.

A Tea Free Trade Zone should be launched under strict customs and regulatory supervision. Investment incentives should attract global tea traders, logistics operators and beverage manufacturers to establish regional operations in Sri Lanka. Simultaneously, a Tea Innovation Centre should focus on future growth categories such as wellness teas, ready-to-drink beverages, nutraceuticals, tea extracts and sustainable packaging solutions. At the same time, smallholders must remain central to the strategy through productivity improvements, replanting support, climate resilience initiatives and access to technology. Transformation will only succeed if growers succeed.

A $ 5 b opportunity

Tea remains one of Sri Lanka’s largest agricultural export industries, yet earnings have largely remained within the $ 1 billion to $ 1.5 billion range for many years. The real opportunity lies beyond production. A carefully designed Tea Hub strategy should target: $ 5 billion tea-sector value by 2035, over $ 500 

million in foreign direct investment, around 50,000 new direct and indirect jobs, significant expansion in packaging, logistics and export services and positioning Colombo emerging as South Asia’s leading tea value-addition and trading centre. These are ambitious goals, but economic transformation has never been achieved through modest ambition.

The moment to be bold

The question before Budget 2027 is not whether Sri Lanka should protect Pure Ceylon Tea. That debate has already been settled. The real question is whether Sri Lanka is prepared to do the reforms and capture a larger share of the wealth generated by the global tea industry. A carefully designed Tea Hub can protect Brand Ceylon while attracting investment, creating employment, strengthening exports and generating new foreign exchange earnings. It can transform tea from a traditional export crop into a modern economic ecosystem. History rarely rewards countries that simply preserve yesterday’s successes. It rewards nations that build tomorrow’s opportunities on the foundations of their greatest strengths.

Next step

Sri Lanka has already earned global recognition for producing some of the finest tea in the world. Budget 2027 offers a far bigger possibility: to transform Sri Lanka from a country that exports tea into the country where the world’s tea business gathers, innovates, trades and creates value. If Singapore became the hub of trade, Dubai the hub of logistics and Switzerland the home of premium food brands, there is no reason Sri Lanka cannot become the global capital of tea. The real risk is not testing this vision. The real risk is allowing the opportunity to pass us by.

(The author has been the Chairman Sri Lanka Export Development Board, served the Tea Board (Marketing) and Chairman of the value added Tea Committee at the Industry and Commerce Ministry. The thoughts are strictly his personal views)

title: Sri Lankan University Rankings: The free fall (Part 2) | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 10 November 2026 00:00
-     - 11

Continued from yesterday

In the first part of this article, I showed that Sri Lanka’s universities sit far below those of countries with similar or even lower incomes, and that the gap widened again in the QS Asia University Rankings 2027, released on 4 November. The University of Colombo, our best, is now 364th in Asia, down from 275th two years ago. Indonesia and Vietnam, at almost exactly our income level, have universities at 53rd and 159th. India, Bangladesh and Pakistan, with half or less of our per capita income, have theirs at 66th, 136th and 76th.

This second part asks the more useful question: why? The QS dataset – 1,722 universities from 26 countries and territories – breaks each university’s score into eleven indicators, showing exactly where we lose our marks.

Where the gap really lies

Comparing Sri Lanka’s top three universities with the top three of each peer country tells us exactly where we fall short. Table III summarises the scores (out of 100).

Four patterns jump out.

nPattern 1: Sri Lanka is closed to the world. This is the single biggest gap. The average score of our top three universities on international faculty is 1.6 out of 100 and on international students 3.8. Inbound and outbound student exchange are similarly close to zero. Indonesia’s flagships score close to 100 on international faculty and on both kinds of exchange; Malaysia’s score 95 or more on all four. Even Bangladesh and Pakistan, hardly magnets for foreign academics, score ten to fifteen times higher than we do on international faculty. Across all 1,722 universities in Asia, the average international faculty score is 33.3. Ours is 1.8.

Put simply, Sri Lankan academics who do research are producing work that is cited. The problem is that there are too few of them, they are overloaded with teaching, they rarely work with foreign colleagues on campus, and they teach almost no foreign students. These are system problems, not individual failings.

The peer scorecard

Table IV compares Sri Lanka’s overall presence in the 2027 Asia rankings with that of its peers. Two numbers stand out. First, Sri Lanka has no university in Asia’s top 200; Vietnam and the Philippines have two each, Bangladesh three, Pakistan five and Indonesia twelve. Second, within South Asia alone – a subregion that QS ranks separately – the University of Colombo is only 83rd. In other words, 82 universities in India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Iran are ahead of our best.

Again, honesty requires a caveat. This year was a difficult one for most of South Asia. About 71% of India’s returning universities, 66% of Pakistan’s and 59% of Bangladesh’s fell in rank, compared with 67% of Sri Lanka’s. IIT Delhi fell from 59th to 66th. The difference is the starting point: a slide from 59th to 66th still leaves IIT Delhi among Asia’s elite; ours moves us further from relevance.

What about research?

The picture is a little better when we look at individual researchers rather than institutions. In the AD Scientific Index, which ranks academics by their Google Scholar citations and h-index, the University of Colombo’s world position improved from 1,655 in early 2025 to 1,315 in mid-2026, and the number of its academics in the global top 10% rose from 21 to 22. Sri Lanka has capable researchers. What it lacks is a system that multiplies their impact: research time, funding, PhD students and international collaboration.

Why is this happening?

Rankings are a symptom. The causes are well known to anyone who has worked with our universities.

The first is money, and what happened to it after 2022. The economic crisis eroded academic salaries in real terms, cut research budgets and accelerated the departure of experienced lecturers abroad. The faculty-student and PhD numbers in the QS data are the statistical footprint of that exodus.

The second is insularity, and it is largely a policy choice. State universities have few incentives to recruit foreign staff or students, and the rules make it hard even when they try. As I pointed out in 2025, visa procedures for foreign academics and students are cumbersome and unpredictable.

The third is weak incentives for research. The research allowance paid to state university academics is largely automatic rather than linked to measurable output. Recruitment and promotion still give limited weight to publication impact. It should not surprise us that output per academic is low.

The fourth is that nobody owns the rankings. Most leading Asian universities have dedicated offices that manage data submissions to ranking agencies, track indicators, build relationships with employers and promote the institution abroad. Few Sri Lankan universities do. The absence of PhD data for five of our ranked universities is a small but telling example: points are being lost simply because data are not submitted.

What our peers did differently

The countries that have overtaken us did not do so by accident. Malaysia made internationalisation a national strategy, opened its doors to foreign branch campuses and set explicit targets for foreign students; its universities now score close to the maximum on every international indicator. Pakistan, through its Higher Education Commission set up in 2002, invested heavily in sending academics abroad for PhDs and in rewarding publications, which is why its flagships score well on research output and staff qualifications despite the country’s economic difficulties. Vietnam allowed ambitious private universities to grow; Duy Tan University, a private institution, is now Vietnam’s highest-ranked university in the QS world table. Indonesia broadened its base, and its top three universities now rank in Asia’s top 60.

The common thread is deliberate policy sustained over a decade or more, not money: none of these countries was richer per head than Sri Lanka when it started. What they had was a decision, made at the top that their universities would compete internationally.

What should be done?

None of this is beyond repair. Countries with fewer resources have moved faster. Here are six practical steps.

Conclusion

Sri Lanka’s universities have long performed below what our income, literacy and history would predict. The 2027 rankings show that the gap is not closing; it is widening. Countries that were poorer than us a decade ago, and some that still are, now have universities that the world takes seriously. Ours are slipping further down the table each year, not because our academics are less able, but because the system around them has stood still while the rest of Asia has moved.

For a country that hopes to sell services, attract investment and keep its talented young people at home that is not an academic concern. It is an economic one. The great fall can still be reversed – but only if we stop treating the rankings as somebody else’s problem.
